result: The porcine cell-free system recapitulates early fertilization proteomic interactions. The system was adapted from Xenopus laevis egg extracts and uses porcine oocytes matured in vitro combined with permeabilized boar spermatozoa. The authors claim this system mimics events that occur during natural fertilization and has been previously validated.
evaluation: All reviewers accept the validity of the cell-free system approach. Reviewer 1 states 'A previous publication of this lab validated the cell-free extract purification methods as recapitulating early events after sperm entry in the oocyte.' Reviewer 3 is 'very positive about the porcine cell-free assay approach and the results presented here.' The editor notes 'The main method used is state-of-the-art and the supporting data are solid.'

result: Mass spectrometry analysis identified 185 proteins that showed statistically significant differences (p<0.1) between control and cell-free-treated spermatozoa across two time points (4 hr and 24 hr). The study used biological triplicates and normalized samples based on outer dense fiber protein content.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the mass spectrometry findings as valid. The editor states 'This important work reports the identification of a list of proteins that may participate in the clearance of paternal mitochondria.' Reviewer 1 notes 'The total number of proteins identified in their test is around 200' without questioning the methodology. Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'They identified a list of 185 proteins that might be candidates for mitophagy determinants.'

result: Proteins were classified into three classes based on their behavior in the cell-free system: Class 1 (oocyte-derived proteins binding to sperm), Class 2 (proteins increasing in abundance), and Class 3 (proteins decreasing in abundance). Class 1 included known oocyte-specific proteins such as zona pellucida proteins 2, 3, and 4, ovastacin, DNA methyltransferase 1, and nucleoplasmin 2.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the classification system and validation through known oocyte proteins. Reviewer 1 notes the system 'allowed the authors to establish a list of proteins either enriched or depleted after incubation with the oocytes extract.' The identification of known oocyte-specific proteins in Class 1 serves as internal validation that reviewers implicitly accept by not questioning it.

result: MVP (Major Vault Protein) was identified as a Class 1 protein, not detected in ejaculated or primed spermatozoa by Western blotting or immunocytochemistry, but detected on sperm tails after 4 and 24 hr of cell-free system exposure. In zygotes, MVP was abundant in cytoplasm at 15 hr post-insemination without associating with male pronuclei or mitochondrial sheaths, but showed colocalization with mitochondrial sheaths at 25 hr post-insemination.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the characterization of MVP. Reviewer 1 states 'Using WB and histochemistry labelling of spermatozoa and early embryos using specific antibodies the authors confirmed the association/dissociation of 6 proteins suspected to be involved in autophagy.' No specific concerns about MVP data are raised by any reviewer.

result: PSMG2 (Proteasome Assembly Chaperone 2) was identified as a Class 2 protein showing significant increase in abundance after 24 hr (p=0.088). It localized to the acrosome in ejaculated spermatozoa, appeared in both head and tail after 4 hr cell-free exposure, returned to head-only localization after 24 hr, and clustered around paternal pronuclei and on mitochondrial sheaths in zygotes at 15 and 25 hr post-insemination.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the PSMG2 characterization as part of the validated set of six proteins. Reviewer 1 confirms 'the authors confirmed the association/dissociation of 6 proteins suspected to be involved in autophagy' using appropriate methods. No specific methodological concerns about PSMG2 are raised.

result: PSMA3 (Proteasome Subunit Alpha 3) significantly increased (p=0.015) during 4 hr trials as a Class 2 protein. It localized to the acrosome in ejaculated spermatozoa, redistributed to the tail after priming and 4 hr cell-free exposure, showed more focused mitochondrial sheath localization after 24 hr, and clustered around pronuclei and on mitochondrial sheaths in zygotes at both 15 and 25 hr post-insemination.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the PSMA3 characterization. Reviewer 1 confirms validation of the six proteins through Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. The editor notes 'the supporting data are solid,' which encompasses these protein characterizations.

result: FUNDC2 (FUN14 Domain-Containing Protein 2) underwent significant decrease in abundance after 4 hr (p=0.084) as a Class 3 protein. It localized to acrosome and mitochondrial sheath in ejaculated spermatozoa, changed localization after capacitation and priming, spread throughout the tail after 4 hr cell-free exposure, returned to a fractured mitochondrial sheath pattern after 24 hr, and was not detected on fertilizing spermatozoa at 15 or 25 hr post-insemination but remained on zona-bound non-fertilizing sperm.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the FUNDC2 characterization. Reviewer 1 confirms the validation approach for all six proteins. The dynamic localization changes and disappearance from fertilizing sperm are not questioned by reviewers.

result: SAMM50 (Sorting and Assembly Machinery Component 50) showed significant decrease in abundance during 4 hr trial (p=0.035) as a Class 3 protein. It localized to acrosome and mitochondrial sheath in ejaculated spermatozoa, persisted on mitochondrial sheath and principal piece after priming and cell-free exposure (4 and 24 hr), localized on/near mitochondrial sheath at 15 hr post-insemination, but was detected only on principal piece (not mitochondrial sheath) at 25 hr post-insemination.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the SAMM50 characterization. Reviewer 1 confirms validation of all six proteins through appropriate methods. The temporal changes in localization are not questioned.

result: BAG5 (BAG Family Molecular Chaperone Regulator 5) decreased in abundance during 4 hr trial (p=0.02) as a Class 3 protein. It localized exclusively to the acrosome in ejaculated spermatozoa, was detectable in acrosome remains and weakly on tail after priming, relocated to mitochondrial sheath after 4 and 24 hr cell-free exposure, but was not observed on fertilizing spermatozoa at 15 or 25 hr post-insemination (though present in zygote cytoplasm).
evaluation: Reviewers accept the BAG5 characterization. Reviewer 1 confirms validation of all six proteins. The dramatic relocalization from acrosome to mitochondrial sheath and subsequent disappearance from fertilizing sperm are not questioned.

result: The 185 identified proteins likely play roles in multiple early fertilization processes beyond sperm mitophagy, including pronuclear development, sperm aster formation, and degradation of various sperm structures. Several autophagy-related proteins (FUNDC2, SAMM50, BAG5) and ubiquitin-proteasome system components were identified.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this limitation. Reviewer 1 states 'The protein identified may also be involved in other processes going on in the oocyte at this time of early development.' Reviewer 2 notes the proteins 'might be candidates for mitophagy determinants (or their co-factors),' indicating acceptance that not all proteins are directly mitophagy-related.

result: This mass spectrometry study represents the first comprehensive proteomic investigation of post-fertilization sperm mitophagy using the porcine cell-free system, identifying candidate proteins for future functional studies. The authors acknowledge that many protein cofactors and pathways remain to be identified.
evaluation: Reviewers recognize the study's value as a starting point but emphasize its limitations. Reviewer 1 states 'this unique approach provides a list of potential proteins involved in sperm mitochondria clearance it is (only) a starting point for many future studies and does not provide the demonstration that any of these proteins has indeed a role in the processes leading to sperm mitochondria clearance.' Reviewer 2 notes 'no further functional validation experiments were performed. Nevertheless, the data presented in the current study is of great interest and could be important for future studies in this field.'

result: The study captures changes in protein abundances only and would not detect proteins that remain at stable abundances but undergo changes in localization or post-translational modifications. The lack of overlap between 4 hr and 24 hr protein inventories may reflect inability to detect dynamic changes.
evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept these limitations by not challenging them. The authors' acknowledgment of these methodological constraints aligns with reviewers' understanding that this is a discovery-phase study providing candidate proteins rather than mechanistic proof.
